lines.text: A narrow land along one river, with ancient stones, a dark past of the slave trade and a young democracy. This is the story of The Gambia.
Over many centuries, people along the river raised more than a thousand circles of standing stones, still standing today.
Europeans came for gold and slaves. On a small island in the river, a fort held captives bound across the Atlantic.
In 1816 the British founded Bathurst at the river's mouth. Today it is the capital, Banjul.
Dawda Jawara would become the first leader of an independent Gambia, and hold office for over thirty years.
Adama Barrow was born, the man who would become president in 2017.
The same year, Yahya Jammeh was born, the soldier who would seize power in 1994.
In 1965, The Gambia became independent from Britain, the smallest country on the African mainland.
In 1976, Alex Haley's book Roots traced his family back to the Gambian village of Juffureh, and moved the world.
From 1982, The Gambia was joined to Senegal in a confederation, which lasted only seven years.
In 2016, Jammeh lost an election and refused to leave, until West African troops arrived and he went into exile.
Along its river, The Gambia has found its voice again.
